title: Monster
content:
You know that feeling when you’re just getting into Anime, and you keep seeing these giant names get brought up in every Anime and Manga discussion, online and between friends. You keep wondering if they really deserve the clout they get.

For completionists, this is often accompanied by a sense of dread that it’s yet another entry you want to check out, and you start freaking out about how old it is, whether it still holds up, how many companion or sequel releases it has for its name and so on. I mean, you start bargaining with time and energy. Yeah, no, if you actually feelthat way hen maybe you have larger mental problems you need to take care of, that is not normal, seek help. If it’s the other way, or at least, to a lesser extreme end, Monster is a deeply disturbing psychological look into a world that has lost its rainbow.

We often look at the later third of the 20th century as cheerful, hopeful, full of unity and optimism for the future. Technology was, as many would consider, its peak. People still had more control, capitalism not as predatory, or at least it did not seem as much, and more than anything, there was this mystic romance to the era. However, Monster paints all of that in a dull, brownish, sometimes blue paint that exposes far more darkness and corruption tied to the world. It creates a romanticized version of central Europe that a lot of media fail to convey. It’s gritty, mysterious, ruthless and dreadful. I mean, who would you fault? The world was changing, a lot of tides were racing to this new future that’s dawning on humanity, but at the same time, many individuals and organizations are still holding on to the old ways.

In a way, Monster makes a very high-risk narrative bet that many other stories tr to dumb down by surrounding it by more vibrant plot points to try numbing the audience a bit to how depressive it might come across. But Monster lays no veil. Here’s the cake with all its frosting, cutlery, and the entire recipe log for you to taste, ponder or and decipher. The question is liquidy and the answers are open ended. The author is not spoon-feeding anything and lets the audience work the cryptic resolution themselves. The entire story feels more like homework than mindless entertainment which is why Monster has a very specific fandom that might feel gated and hard to get into.

One very interesting block among what makes Monster stand out are the characters. Sure, people like to pick favorites, personify them and project themselves onto them. Fine, every other Anime comes up with this quirk already, but the characters in Monster really are no more than primary vessels to different ideas and ideologies. It’s not about Johan and Dr. Tenma at the end of the day; it’s about something far deeper and condescending. Good vs. Evil? Optimism vs. Pessimism? Existentialism vs. Nihilism? The author laid down all the pieces, the timeline and the vessels. Everything else is just pattern matching and placeholder swapping really, there is no concrete start or end, just how sharp and cynical the audience’s mind is.

One thing for sure. Monster is not a show for everyone. It can be a gripping murder mystery with more suspense than frames per second, or a snooze fest slower than your average seasonal Isekai cookie-cutter. It’s a mindset before being an Anime. But hey, that’s not necessarily a bad thing.

Overall: 8.24/10.
